blocks.text: SESSION 1 — Concept · Key Points · Memory Technique. Read, absorb, stop.
1. Concept Explained Simply

TOGAF draws a precise three-way distinction between output types: **Deliverable** = the formal, contractually agreed output. **Artifact** = a specific work product describing one aspect of the architecture (lives inside a deliverable). **Building Block** = a reusable component assembled to form architectures and solutions.

Building blocks split into two subtypes: **ABB** (Architecture Building Block) = describes what capability is needed (implementation-independent). **SBB** (Solution Building Block) = describes how that capability is actually delivered (the real product/component).
The nesting relationship: **Deliverable contains Artifacts → Artifacts describe Building Blocks.**
2. Key Points to Remember

items: **Deliverable**: Contractually specified; formally reviewed, approved, signed off; archived at project completion. Examples: Architecture Definition Document, Statement of Architecture Work.
**Artifact** — three types (**CMD**): Catalog (list of things) · Matrix (relationships between things) · Diagram (pictures of things)
**ABB**: "Identity and Access Management capability" — no vendor named
**SBB**: "Azure Active Directory via SAML 2.0" — specific product chosen

blocks.text: 3. Memory Technique

The Russian Doll: Deliverable (outer — stakeholders sign off) → Artifact (middle — specific diagram/list/matrix) → Building Block (inner — reusable component).

ABB vs SBB — "what vs which": ABB = What capability? (no vendor) · SBB = Which product? (specific)

CMD artifacts: Catalog (list) · Matrix (relationships) · Diagram (picture)
EXAM TRAP — An artifact may or may not be a deliverable — it depends on whether it is contractually specified. Not every artifact is a deliverable, and not every deliverable is just one artifact.
✋ PAUSE POINT — CHECK BEFORE CONTINUING. Answer from memory before reading Session 2.
1. What is the defining characteristic of a Deliverable that distinguishes it from an Artifact?

A Deliverable is contractually specified and formally reviewed, approved, and signed off by stakeholders. An Artifact is a work product describing one aspect of architecture — it may or may not be contractually specified.
2. Name the three types of Artifact and what each one shows.
Catalog (list of things), Matrix (relationships between things), Diagram (pictures of things) — CMD.
3. What is the key distinction between an ABB and an SBB?
ABB describes required capability with no specific product named (implementation-independent). SBB represents an actual implementation choice — a specific product or component.
SESSION 2 — Real-World Example · Practice Questions · Part 2 Scenario
4. Real-World Example — ServiceNow ITSM
**Deliverables**: The signed-off ITSM Design Document, Integration Specification, Data Migration Plan — formally reviewed and archived.
**Artifacts**: Catalog — list of all ITSM processes in scope; Matrix — mapping ServiceNow applications to business processes; Diagram — swimlane diagram showing the Incident Management workflow.
**Building Blocks**: ABB — "Identity Integration capability" (no product named). SBB — "Azure AD via SAML 2.0 with MID Server sync" (specific implementation).
5. Part 1 Practice Questions
Q1. Which best describes a TOGAF Deliverable?

items: A) Any diagram produced during the ADM
B) A reusable component combined with others to deliver architectures
C) A work product that is contractually specified and formally reviewed, approved, and signed off ✓
D) A list of architectural standards in the Architecture Repository

blocks.text: Answer: C — the contractual, formally signed-off nature defines a Deliverable.
Q2. An architect produces an Application Interaction Matrix in Phase C. How should it be classified?

items: A) A deliverable, because it is produced during a formal ADM phase
B) A building block, because it describes application components
C) An artifact — specifically a matrix type — because it shows relationships between things ✓
D) A Solution Building Block

blocks.text: Answer: C — produced in a formal phase does not make it a deliverable.
Q3. What is the key distinction between an ABB and an SBB?

items: A) ABBs are used in Business Architecture; SBBs are used in Technology Architecture
B) ABBs describe required capability and are implementation-independent; SBBs represent actual implementation choices ✓
C) ABBs are created in Phase A; SBBs in Phase E
D) ABBs are reusable; SBBs cannot be reused

blocks.text: Answer: B — ABB = what capability; SBB = which product.
6. Part 2 Scenario Question

SCENARIO: GlobalTech's architecture team has produced: (1) a signed Architecture Definition Document approved by the Architecture Board; (2) a Data Entity Catalog listing all master data objects to be migrated; (3) a diagram showing how Dynamics 365 integrates with the HR system; (4) a requirement for a "Master Data Management capability" — vendor not yet selected; (5) a decision to implement that capability using Azure Data Factory.
Question: Classify each of the five outputs using correct TOGAF terminology. Justify each classification in one sentence.

items: **Architecture Definition Document → Deliverable** — formally reviewed, approved, and signed off by the Architecture Board.
**Data Entity Catalog → Artifact (Catalog type)** — a list of data entities describing an aspect of the Data Architecture; lives inside the deliverable.
**Integration diagram → Artifact (Diagram type)** — a picture of application interactions describing an aspect of the Application Architecture.
**"Master Data Management capability" → ABB** — describes a required capability in an implementation-independent way; no product named.
**Azure Data Factory → SBB** — the actual implementation choice made to realise the MDM capability defined in the ABB.

blocks.text: Fold-In: Architecture Patterns (ADM Techniques Ch.4)

Closely related to Building Blocks: a pattern is "an idea that has been useful in one practical context and will probably be useful in others" (M. Fowler). In TOGAF terms, patterns are a way of putting Building Blocks into context — Building Blocks are what you use; patterns tell you how, when, why, and what trade-offs apply. A pattern helps identify combinations of ABBs/SBBs proven to deliver effective solutions before.

A typical pattern documents: Name (memorable reference) · Problem (the goals to reach) · Context (preconditions) · Forces (competing constraints and trade-offs, e.g. security vs performance vs scalability) · Solution (structure and behaviour) · Resulting Context (what's resolved, what remains open) · Examples and Known Uses.

EXAM TRAP — Don't confuse an Architecture Pattern (a reusable enterprise-level solution structure, TOGAF's usage) with a Design Pattern (a software-specific, code-level recurring structure) or an Idiom (a language-specific low-level pattern). TOGAF patterns concern enterprise information systems — software, hardware, networks, and people — not purely software design.
